headline: Every major is ripping above its 200-day line except XRP and DOGE, and RSI is screaming overbought while the crowd still reads Fear
paragraphs: Start with the regime, because it moved. Five of the seven majors here, BTC, ETH, SOL, BNB, are above their 200-day averages, and XRP and DOGE are still below theirs despite double-digit daily gains. That is a market where the broad trend has turned up but the laggards haven't confirmed it yet. ADA sits below its 200-day too, and it's the only one whose MACD hasn't crossed bullish, still below its signal line even after a 6.79% day. When six out of seven names post double-digit or near-double-digit gains and the trend lines don't all agree, you have a fast move, not yet a settled one.

Momentum is where this gets interesting. BTC's RSI-14 is 73.7, SOL's is 74.8, and ETH's is 82.1: all three are deep in overbought territory by any classical read. ETH's 24-hour move of 17.28% on top of a 17.69% seven-day gain is the kind of acceleration that usually front-runs a pause, not because charts predict anything, but because RSI above 80 has historically meant the move is stretched, not that it's over. XRP and ADA are the exceptions, sitting at 62.4 and 56.2 RSI respectively, gains without the overheating, which tracks with them still being under their 200-day lines. Everything here says: strong trend, hot momentum, uneven confirmation.

Positioning tells you this rally isn't cheap anymore. Funding across BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP, and DOGE is uniformly 0.01% per 8 hours (about 11% annualized), meaning longs are paying shorts to stay in the trade, a modest but real cost of being bullish on leverage. Open interest is heaviest in BTC ($2.13B) and ETH ($1.35B), and the long/short account ratios lean long everywhere, most extreme in DOGE (4.24) and XRP (2.55). Liquidations confirm who's been squeezed: shorts have absorbed the pain by a wide margin across every asset, $14M in BTC shorts liquidated in 8 hours versus $2.1M longs, $17.6M in SOL shorts versus $1.4M longs. This has been a short squeeze as much as a rally, crowded positioning on the losing side getting forced out, which adds fuel but also fragility if the move stalls.

Flows are where the picture splits. Spot ETF money is still arriving: BTC funds took in $164.2M on August 19th, $463.7M over the last five sessions, with three straight days in the same direction. ETH ETFs added $17.7M on the day, $125.9M over five sessions, also three days running. That's real traditional-finance demand showing up in the tape. But the 24-hour whale ledger shows something calmer: $0 net moving off exchanges today, with the single largest tracked move being $189.9M in USDT going onto Binance, stablecoin firepower parking itself at an exchange rather than volatile coins leaving custody. Zoom out to the weekly trend and the last two readings flipped to onto-exchanges ($1.05B and $70M), a reversal from the two prior weeks that saw over $2.2B combined move off exchanges into cold storage. Stablecoin float itself is essentially flat, down 0.52% over 30 days, so the dry powder isn't growing, it's just repositioning.

Sentiment is the foil here and it's a loud one. Fear & Greed reads 46, labeled Fear, sitting at the top of its own 30-day range of 25 to 46. So the crowd's mood gauge has recovered to its best reading in a month, yet still calls itself fearful, while the actual price action, ETF flows, and short liquidations all look like conviction. That gap between what the gauge says and what the tape shows is worth sitting with rather than resolving. Total market cap is up 7.27% on the day to $2.459T, BTC dominance holds at 56.6%, and the day's leaderboard (TRUMP +24.4%, HYPE +20.3%, ARB +19.1%) reads like risk appetite broadly, not a single-asset story. What to watch from here: whether funding stays this cheap as the rally extends (a jump toward richer annualized funding would mean the crowded long book is paying up), whether XRP and DOGE actually reclaim their 200-day lines rather than just approaching them, and whether the whale ledger's tilt back toward exchanges over the last two weekly readings turns into a third.
